title: The unforgiving servant
hook: a man forgiven a huge debt throttles someone over a small one (Matthew 18:23–35)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter's question and the answer that took the counting away. Your line was a number too big to keep track of. Did you catch the tally starting up again? Today, the story Jesus tells right after that answer. Day nine hundred forty-nine.

A king sits down to go through his accounts, and one servant is brought in owing him ten thousand talents. The text says plainly he has nothing to pay it with. The king orders him sold, with his wife and children and everything he has. The servant falls down before him and begs: be patient, I'll pay it all. And the king, moved with compassion, lets him go and forgives the whole debt. The servant walks out a free man. Then he goes out, and what he does next is the whole story. Today: the unforgiving servant.
screen: `TEN THOUSAND TALENTS.` → `BE PATIENT, I'LL PAY IT ALL.` → `THE WHOLE DEBT, FORGIVEN.`

segments.voice: First, the turn. Outside, the forgiven servant runs into a fellow servant who owes him an hundred pence, in the King James words. A small sum, set right beside an impossible one. And the text says he "laid hands on him, and took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest." The fellow servant falls down and begs with almost the same words: "Have patience with me, and I will pay thee all." The same plea that just saved the first man. He refuses, and has him thrown in prison until he pays. Second, the witnesses. The other servants see it, and they're very sorry, and they go and tell the king everything. The story doesn't let this happen in private. Mercy, and the lack of it, gets noticed. Third, the question at the center. The king calls the man back and asks: "Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?" Even as I had pity on thee. That's the whole parable in one line. The servant's problem isn't that he wanted his money. It's that he walked out of the biggest mercy of his life and didn't let it change a single thing about how he treated anyone else. Fourth, the hard ending. The king hands him over to the tormentors, and Jesus closes with a warning about forgiving a brother from the heart. Christians read that ending differently. Some take it as a stark warning about judgment. Others hear it as a picture of what an unforgiving heart already does to itself: it locks itself in. Both readings keep the same center. The man forgot he had been forgiven.
screen: `BY THE THROAT, OVER A SMALL DEBT.` · `THE OTHER SERVANTS SEE IT.` · `EVEN AS I HAD PITY ON THEE.` · `A HARD ENDING, READ TWO WAYS.` · then, large: `SHOULDEST NOT THOU ALSO HAVE HAD COMPASSION?`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind a time someone let you off. A parent who didn't stay angry. A friend who took you back. A teacher who gave a second chance, a boss who let a mistake go, a stranger who was kind when you'd been rude. Stay with that memory for a minute. What did you owe them? What did they choose not to collect? Then, gently, let someone come to mind who owes you something small today. Hold the two side by side, the way the story does. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own tradition's words for the mercy you received. The bell holds the time.
Talents. The enormous debt, ten thousand of them, that a king forgave a servant who then seized a fellow servant over a small one. Today's word.
Your line: I was forgiven too. Today, the next time someone's small debt gets under your skin, remember one time you were let off, before you say anything. Day nine hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians read the parable of the unforgiving servant as part of Jesus's answer to Peter about forgiveness, since Matthew places it right after seventy times seven.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a man who was mean about money.
what it means: a man forgiven everything who walked out of that mercy without letting it change him.
what a scholar hears: Matthew sets the parable right after seventy times seven, and the fellow servant's plea echoes the first servant's almost word for word.

notes: The sums (ten thousand talents, an hundred pence) are the text's own; no modern value is given on purpose.
Matthew 18:26 (first servant's plea) in the KJV reads 'Lord, have patience with me, and I will pay thee all'; the voice says 'be patient, I'll pay it all' as a paraphrase in the hook.
Two readings of the ending (18:34–35) given without ranking; a Christian Keeper should confirm they're fairly put.
'He has nothing to pay it with' paraphrases 18:25 ('he had not to pay').
Editor pass: hook embellishments cut ('dragged in', 'everyone in the room knows it', 'a sum nobody could ever pay'); now follows 18:24–25 more closely.
Audit (2026-10-01): hook 'falls on his face' corrected to 'falls down before him' (Matthew 18:26 KJV: 'fell down, and worshipped him').
